citations.sentence: Two projects, The Music Bible and TheSinging.Bible, say AI now sings every chapter of the Bible, but we found no published error rates from either [1] [2].
citations.note: Lede added after the writer's draft (SEO/format step). Absence claim reworded per factcheck-round2.json.

citations.sentence: Between mid-September and mid-October, two separate projects ... kept growing, and new survey data showed why many pastors remain cautious.
TheSinging.Bible, which launched on Aug 25, added an iPhone app on Sept 21, a round-the-clock YouTube radio stream on Oct 2 and an Android app on Oct 4.
As of Oct 4, it lists 52,316 recordings: all 1,189 chapters in 22 styles, each sung in a male and a female voice.
Answered Faith reported in September that it launched with 38,048 recordings.
We noted The Music Bible's app launch in our Sep 30 issue.
citations.note: Added per editor; internal reference to content/faith/2026-09-30-kairos-ai-bible-chatbot.md.

citations.sentence: Since then, on Oct 8, Crosswalk ran a guest commentary on the app, which is led by founder Micah Fiechter.
Crosswalk reported Fiechter saying the whole Bible is available in 11 styles, and it put the app at more than 30,000 songs, with three genres in Spanish.
Three days later, the headline of Fiechter's own op-ed put the figure at 38,000.
citations.note: Type set back to Official per editor (first-party statement); outlet keeps '(op-ed by Micah Fiechter)'.

citations.sentence: The app's homepage counter now reads 38,556.
The counts differ by source and date, and we found no outside check of them.
Table: Music Bible 38,556 songs; 14 complete-Bible genres, counting Spanish.
Table: TheSinging.Bible 52,316 recordings; 22 styles, two voices; Singing Bible Edition; AI-empowered technologies; free, no sign-up, no ads.
Table: Music Bible English text not named on the pages we read.
Table: Suno and ChatGPT, among others.
Table: Music Bible free on iOS and Android.
The Music Bible says AI shapes the music, not the words.
citations.note: Supported by the [2] sentences that follow.

citations.sentence: It pledges it "will never use artificial intelligence to create songs that interpret, paraphrase, or extrapolate the meaning of Scripture."
It says verses stay in order with no choruses, though "occasionally, a word or phrase may be repeated for musical expression."
TheSinging.Bible makes a narrower claim: "every recording follows the written text, which is shown with every chapter."
The project says producers, engineers and quality-control reviewers were responsible for reviewing the recordings.
"We don't change Scripture to fit music; we change music to fit Scripture," Fiechter told Crosswalk.
The Music Bible argues that setting the whole Bible, "over 750,000 words," to music was more than any single artist or team could do by hand.
Both projects are built for listening, and The Music Bible also pitches memorizing.
citations.note: 'Memorize' evidence from factcheck.json, not in claim ledger.

citations.sentence: TheSinging.Bible says under 20 minutes a day sings a listener through the whole Bible in a year, with the text on screen.
Its book of Jonah is even available as a sea shanty.
The Music Bible app offers read-along lyrics and playlists that AI builds from a short text request.
"I don't want people to remember Music Bible; I want them to remember the Bible," Fiechter said.
We found no published error rates from either project.
Answered Faith noted that TheSinging.Bible's release did not "publish detailed error rates from its quality-control process."
The Music Bible commits to "at least 100% accuracy in the oral representation of each passage," but its page describes no review method.
TheSinging.Bible's one million plays in two weeks come from its own analytics, and "a play should not be confused with a unique listener or a completed chapter."
On Oct 6, Barna reported that 33% of Protestant pastors feel positive about AI writing worship songs and 29% about AI interpreting scripture, compared with 64% for AI creating small-group curriculum.
The survey of 442 pastors was conducted online in December 2025.
We found no mention of sung Scripture in Barna's report. The Music Bible says AI writes only the music, so it falls between these categories.
On Oct 13, Movieguide followed up on how AI helps translate The Chosen.
citations.note: Date confirmed in factcheck-round2.json; supported by the [9] sentence that follows.

citations.sentence: Citing a fact sheet, it reports that for subtitles "a trained subject matter expert examines each line for accuracy, biblical fidelity and cultural relevance."
citations.note: Per factcheck-round2.json: Movieguide's own text, attributed to a fact sheet, describing subtitle review only (not dubbing). Phrase confirmed via fetch tool (curl 403).

citations.sentence: The wider workflow was first reported by Deseret News in May: Come and See uses an AI app for a first-pass translation in minority languages, then speech-to-speech AI lays the original actor's voice over recordings made by linguists.
citations.note: Source 10 switched from the KSL syndicated copy (2026-06-01) to the Deseret News original (2026-05-30) per factcheck-round2.json; title unchanged and confirmed.

citations.sentence: The goal is 600 languages, more than 500 of them with no existing dubbing infrastructure.
At Gloo's fourth annual AI hackathon, held Oct 6-8, Biola University's team Holy Sound reached the finals with a tool that lets people use natural language to run sound boards.
citations.note: Location, participant counts and prizes omitted (geography; avoid repeating 2026-10-11 issue). No 'prototype' or 'volunteers'.
